title: Resolve your own species names
text: Here we present a practical guide to the flora_search() and flora_match() functions of the floraR package. Unlike flora_records(), which browses the checklist itself, these two functions take a list of names you already have — from your own herbarium, field survey, or collaborator — and resolve them against the Flora e Funga do Brasil (FFB) checklist.

title: Resolve your own species names
section: flora_search(): resolve a single name list
text:
flora_search(): resolve a single name list
flora_search() matches each name in a character vector against the FFB checklist. It tries an exact match first; if none is found, it falls back to a fuzzy (generalized Levenshtein-distance) match, which is what catches typos and minor spelling variants. When several checklist entries could match, the one classified "NOME_ACEITO" (accepted) is preferred, so synonyms are automatically resolved to their accepted name.

Arguments







Argument
Description




splist
Character vector of plant names to search.


version
FFB dataset version to use. Defaults to "latest".


max_distance
Maximum edit distance allowed for a fuzzy match — an integer number of edits, or a fraction of name length (e.g. 0.2 allows roughly 1 edit per 5 characters). Default 0.2.


show_correct
If TRUE, appends a Correct column flagging exact (TRUE) vs. fuzzy (FALSE) matches.


genus_fuzzy
If FALSE (default), the genus must match exactly and only the epithet is fuzzily matched — considerably faster for large lists.


progress_bar
If TRUE, shows a progress bar.


rm_flora_database
If TRUE, deletes the cached database after searching. Default FALSE is recommended for repeated use.





Examples
library(floraR)

# A single accepted name
flora_search("Mimosa sensitiva")

# A misspelled epithet, flagging exact vs. fuzzy matches
flora_search("Mimosa sensittiva", max_distance = 0.2, show_correct = TRUE)

# A synonym - resolves to the accepted name automatically
flora_search("Mimosa pyrenea")

# A whole list at once
splist <- c("Mimosa sensitiva", "Swartzia simplex", "Inga edulis")
flora_search(splist, show_correct = TRUE, progress_bar = TRUE)

title: Resolve your own species names
section: flora_match(): compare two independent name lists
text:
flora_match(): compare two independent name lists
flora_match() searches two name lists independently with flora_search(), then aligns entries from both lists that resolve to the same accepted taxon — even when one or both sides used a synonym. This is useful for checking your species list against a collaborator’s, or reconciling two datasets that used different nomenclature.

Arguments







Argument
Description




splist1, splist2
Character vectors — the reference list and the list to match against it.


include_all
If TRUE (default), names found only in splist2 are appended to the result.


identify_dups
If TRUE (default), flags rows where two input names are synonyms of the same accepted taxon.


show_correct, genus_fuzzy, max_distance, version, rm_flora_database, progress_bar
Same meaning as in flora_search().





Example
splist1 <- c("Mimosa sensitiva", "Swartzia simplex", "Inga edulis")
splist2 <- c("Swartzia simplex var. grandiflora", "Inga edulis", "Mimosa pyrenea")

result <- flora_match(splist1, splist2, include_all = TRUE)

# Re-order splist2 to align with splist1
splist2[result$Match.Position.2to1]

title: Resolve your own species names
text:
Additional Tips

Keep rm_flora_database = FALSE (the default) across a session: the first flora_search()/flora_match() call downloads and parses the FFB dataset, and every subsequent call reuses that cache — repeated searches become nearly instant.
Use show_correct = TRUE when auditing a name list, so you can review every fuzzy match manually rather than trusting it blindly.
flora_match()’s Duplicated.Output.Position column is useful for spotting when two of your own names turn out to be synonyms of each other.

title: Curate and describe new records
text: Here we present a practical guide to the flora_get_descriptions() and flora_build_matrix() functions of the floraR package. Together, they support taxonomic experts curating and updating Flora e Funga do Brasil (FFB) records, by extracting existing taxon descriptions and turning them into a structured, comparable format.

title: Curate and describe new records
text:
flora_get_descriptions(): scrape taxon-page descriptions
For each taxon supplied, flora_get_descriptions() downloads a printable PDF version of its FFB taxon page, extracts the text, and searches it for two kinds of descriptions: controlled-field descriptions (“Descrição com campos controlados”) and free-text descriptions (“Descrição livre”).

Arguments







Argument
Description




taxa
A data frame with at least the columns genus, specificEpithet, and references (a link to each taxon’s FFB page) — for example, the output of flora_records().


delay
Numeric. Seconds to wait for the page to load before capturing the PDF. Default 10.


verbose
Logical. If TRUE (default), prints progress messages.





Value
A named list with descriptions_controlled and descriptions_free, each a named list of extracted description text keyed by scientific name. If any taxon page fails to parse, that element instead becomes a two-part list: the successfully extracted descriptions, plus a character vector of the taxa that failed.


Example
library(floraR)

taxa <- flora_records(taxon = "Luetzelburgia",
                      taxonomicStatus = "NOME_ACEITO")

descriptions <- flora_get_descriptions(taxa, delay = 10)

title: Curate and describe new records
section: flora_build_matrix(): turn descriptions into a trait matrix
text:
flora_build_matrix(): turn descriptions into a trait matrix
flora_build_matrix() converts the description text extracted by flora_get_descriptions() into a character matrix — taxa as rows, character states as columns — ready for downstream comparison or trait analysis. It expects the semi-structured description format used on FFB taxon pages, where character categories are separated by periods, category names are separated from their values by colons, and multiple states are separated by semicolons.

Arguments







Argument
Description




descriptions
A named list of description strings, typically one element of the output of flora_get_descriptions() (e.g. descriptions[[1]]).





Example
trait_matrix <- flora_build_matrix(descriptions[[1]])

title: Curate and describe new records
text:
Full workflow
library(floraR)

taxa <- flora_get_children_taxa(taxon_name = "Luetzelburgia",
                                rank = "genus",
                                child_rank = "species")

descriptions <- flora_get_descriptions(taxa, delay = 10)
trait_matrix <- flora_build_matrix(descriptions[[1]])

title: Curate and describe new records
text:
Additional Tips

flora_get_descriptions() scrapes live web pages, so it is slower than the other floraR functions and should be run on a curated, not overly long, taxon list rather than the whole checklist.
Increase delay if you notice missing or truncated descriptions — some taxon pages take longer to render before the printable PDF is captured.
flora_build_matrix() uses the first description in the list to define the expected matrix structure and column names, so make sure that first entry follows the standard semi-structured format before running it on the full set.

title: Find species missing from FFB
text:
Here we present a practical guide to the flora_species_gap() function of the floraR package. Given a genus of plants or algae, it lists the species-level names that occur in Brazil but that the Flora e Funga do Brasil (FFB) does not register yet - a to-do list for taxonomists expanding the FFB monographs.
It combines two independent kinds of evidence that a species occurs in Brazil:
The result is a single table, one row per name, stating which source(s) reported it. Names reported by both are listed first: they are the strongest candidates for inclusion in FFB.

title: Find species missing from FFB
text:
How the comparison works

FFB side. Read every name currently registered in FFB, from the locally cached FFB dataset (downloaded only when needed, as in flora_download()).
Each source. Retrieve the genus’s species-level names - accepted names and synonyms - with each name’s accepted name, and the evidence that it occurs in Brazil.
Missing names. Keep only the names not already in FFB. A name counts as already in FFB when either the name itself or its accepted name matches any FFB name, anywhere in the checklist. This matters because checklists disagree on generic placement: for example, POWO lists Myrcia doloresensis as a synonym of Eugenia florida, which FFB registers under Eugenia.
One table. Merge the names from both sources into one row per name.

Names are compared ignoring case, diacritics, hyphens, y/i, and the genitive -ii/-i ending, so orthographic variants are neither reported as missing nor listed twice. For example, POWO’s Luetzelburgia andrade-limae is recognised as FFB’s L. andradelimae, and POWO’s Myrcia aegiphylloides is merged with GBIF’s Myrcia aegyphylloides. Only species-level names are reported.

title: Find species missing from FFB
text:
Where the evidence comes from

POWO distributions (sources = "powo")
POWO’s names, synonymy, and distribution maps all come from the World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP). POWO’s own API blocks programmatic clients, so Kew’s data is read from one of two places, chosen with powo_source:



powo_source
What it reads
Speed




"rWCVPdata" (default)
The whole WCVP, installed locally by the rWCVPdata package.
Fast: every name and distribution of the genus is resolved at once, in memory.


"checklistbank"
POWO’s own weekly export and WCVP, as hosted on ChecklistBank.
Slower: one web request per candidate. Always current, and needs no extra package.



A species has POWO evidence when its accepted name occurs in at least one of the five TDWG level-3 areas covering Brazil - Brazil North, Northeast, West-Central, Southeast, and South - the areas POWO maps. If no distribution is mapped, POWO’s free-text range (e.g. "Brazil (Bahia)") is checked instead; POWO_Evidence_Source records which was used. POWO covers vascular plants only, so it finds nothing for algae.


GBIF type specimens (sources = "gbif")
The genus is searched among plants and algae only - the GBIF kingdoms Plantae (land plants, red and green algae), Chromista (brown algae, diatoms), and Protozoa (euglenids) - so a genus name shared with an animal, such as Gracilaria (both a red alga and a moth), resolves to the alga. A single search lists every name in the genus with type specimens collected in Brazil; for the FFB-missing names only, the specimens themselves are then retrieved and summarised.

title: Find species missing from FFB
text:
Installing rWCVPdata
rWCVPdata is not on CRAN. Install it once with:
install.packages("rWCVPdata",
                 repos = c("https://matildabrown.github.io/drat",
                           "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
The WCVP version in use is shown in each HTML report; rWCVPdata::wcvp_check_version() tells you whether a newer release is available. If you prefer not to install it, use powo_source = "checklistbank", or sources = "gbif".

title: Find species missing from FFB
text:
Find species missing from FFB
library(floraR)

gap <- flora_species_gap(taxon = "Myrcia")
This returns one row per missing name, and also saves an .xlsx spreadsheet and a self-contained HTML report (KPI counts plus a filterable table you can copy or download) in the flora_species_gap/ folder. For Myrcia, 28 names are missing from FFB: 6 reported by both POWO and GBIF - such as Myrcia microcalyx, mapped by POWO in Brazil North and known from a holotype and isotypes collected there - 4 by POWO only, and 18 by GBIF only.
Key columns of the result:







Column
Meaning




Taxon_name, Authors, Accepted_name
The name, its authors, and its accepted name.


Found_in
"POWO; GBIF", "POWO", or "GBIF".


Brazil_evidence
Whether POWO places the species in Brazil or it has Brazilian types.


POWO_Brazil_Areas, POWO_Evidence_Source
The Brazilian regions POWO maps for the species, and whether from the WCVP distribution or POWO’s range text.


POWO_Published_in, POWO_URL, IPNI_URL
Protologue citation, and links to the name’s POWO and IPNI pages.


GBIF_N_type_specimens, GBIF_Type_statuses
Number of type specimens collected in Brazil, and their categories.


GBIF_Type_specimens
Up to ten specimens, as herbarium, catalogue number, and type status.


GBIF_Specimen_names
The names the types are filed under in GBIF - usually the typified name.


GBIF_Collectors, GBIF_Years, GBIF_States
Who collected the types, when, and in which Brazilian states.


GBIF_URL
Link to the name’s GBIF page.



Source-specific columns are NA for names the other source did not report.

title: Find species missing from FFB
text:
Read the typification
GBIF_Specimen_names shows which name each type actually belongs to, which often differs from Taxon_name. For example, in Myrcia the row for Myrcia aegiphylloides (reported by both sources) rests on a holotype collected in Rio de Janeiro that GBIF files under Aulomyrcia anomala O.Berg - pointing straight to the basionym and its original material.

title: Find species missing from FFB
section: Use one source at a time
text:
Use one source at a time
# POWO only, read live from ChecklistBank
gap_powo <- flora_species_gap(taxon = "Myrcia", sources = "powo",
                              powo_source = "checklistbank")

# GBIF only - e.g. for algae, which POWO does not cover
gap_algae <- flora_species_gap(taxon = "Gracilaria", sources = "gbif")

# Stricter type evidence: holotypes and isotypes only
gap_strict <- flora_species_gap(taxon = "Myrcia", type_status = c("Holotype", "Isotype"))

# Also review POWO names missing from FFB that POWO places outside Brazil
gap_all <- flora_species_gap(taxon = "Myrcia", require_brazil_evidence = FALSE)

title: Parse FFB Darwin Core Archives
text: Here we present a practical guide to the flora_parse() function of the floraR package. This function reads and organizes locally downloaded Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A) datasets from Flora e Funga do Brasil (FFB), turning the raw archive files into a clean, ready-to-use list of tables. It is the second step in the workflow, after flora_download().

title: Parse FFB Darwin Core Archives
Parse FFB Darwin Core Archives
text:
Arguments







Argument
Description




path
Character. Path to the local directory where the versioned FFB DwC-A folders were downloaded (usually created by flora_download()).


version
Character. "latest" parses the most recent downloaded version; "all" parses every downloaded version; a version string or vector parses specific versions.


verbose
Logical. If TRUE (default), prints informative progress messages.

title: Parse FFB Darwin Core Archives
text:
Output structure
flora_parse() returns a named list, one element per versioned folder (e.g. "dwca_ffb_v393_418"), each containing:

$meta: metadata describing the dataset structure.
$data: a nested list of parsed Darwin Core tables, including taxon.txt (with the new taxonName field), distribution.txt (with endemism and phytogeographicDomain columns), and speciesprofile.txt (with lifeForm, habitat, and vegetationType columns).

title: Parse FFB Darwin Core Archives
text:
Parse the latest downloaded version
library(floraR)

# Step 1 - download (skip if already downloaded)
flora_download(version = "latest", dir = "flora_download")

# Step 2 - parse (works offline once downloaded)
dwca <- flora_parse(path = "flora_download", version = "latest")

# Step 3 - explore the parsed structure
names(dwca)
names(dwca[["dwca_ffb_v393_418"]][["data"]])

text:
Access individual tables
taxon_data        <- dwca[["dwca_ffb_v393_418"]][["data"]][["taxon.txt"]]
distribution_data <- dwca[["dwca_ffb_v393_418"]][["data"]][["distribution.txt"]]
profile_data       <- dwca[["dwca_ffb_v393_418"]][["data"]][["speciesprofile.txt"]]

title: Parse FFB Darwin Core Archives
text:
Additional Tips

You rarely need to call flora_parse() directly: flora_records() and the name-resolution functions call it automatically and reuse the cached, parsed result on repeated calls.
Because parsing works offline, it is a good way to inspect the raw structure of a dataset version without re-downloading it.
The generated taxonName field is the same clean binomial used internally by flora_search() for name matching, so it is a reliable join key if you need to merge FFB data with your own tables.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
What is Flora e Funga do Brasil?
Flora e Funga do Brasil (FFB) is the taxonomic checklist that documents Brazil’s plant, algal, and fungal diversity — the richest in the world. Maintained by the Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden and curated collaboratively by hundreds of taxonomists, it records accepted names, synonyms, taxonomic classification, geographic distribution, endemism, life form, habitat, and vegetation type for every documented species.


What can I use floraR for?
The floraR package lets researchers and taxonomists download, parse, filter, and explore the Flora e Funga do Brasil checklist directly from R. You can browse the checklist by taxonomic, geographic, or trait-based criteria, resolve your own species name lists against it (with fuzzy matching for typos), explore the taxonomic hierarchy, and curate new records for contribution back to FFB. Beyond retrieving data, it helps taxonomists expand the FFB monographs: flora_species_gap() finds species recorded in Brazil - by Plants of the World Online distributions or by type specimens collected in Brazil (GBIF) - that FFB does not list yet, and flora_distribution_gap() finds Brazilian states with specimen evidence missing from a taxon’s FFB distribution.


Does floraR cover fungi?
No. floraR works with the plant and algal data of Flora e Funga do Brasil. For fungi, use its companion package fungaR.


Do I need a list of species names to use floraR?
No. flora_records() lets you browse and filter the FFB checklist directly (e.g. all accepted species in a family, or all endemics in a given state) without providing any input names. If you already have your own species list — from a herbarium, field survey, or collaborator — flora_search() and flora_match() resolve those names against the checklist instead, with exact matching first and fuzzy (Levenshtein-distance) matching as a fallback for typos.


Does floraR require an internet connection?
Only the first time you query a given dataset version. flora_download() and flora_parse() fetch and cache the versioned Darwin Core Archive locally, and every other function reuses that cache automatically, so repeated queries and offline analysis work without a new download. The exceptions are the curation tools flora_species_gap() and flora_distribution_gap(), which query online sources (GBIF, and ChecklistBank if chosen) every time they run.


How do I install floraR?
Visit the Get Started guide for installation instructions from GitHub.


Is floraR free to use?
Yes. floraR is open source, licensed under the MIT License.


Is this website available in Portuguese?
Yes. Every page has an EN/PT toggle in the navigation bar. Once you switch languages, the choice is remembered for the rest of your visit — you won’t need to switch again as you navigate between pages.


What output can floraR generate?
floraR returns tidy data frames (and, for flora_parse(), a structured list of DwC-A tables) ready for downstream analysis. flora_records() and flora_get_children_taxa() can also save results directly to CSV, and flora_build_matrix() produces a taxon-by-character trait matrix for comparative or phylogenetic analyses. The curation tools flora_species_gap() and flora_distribution_gap() also save an .xlsx spreadsheet and a self-contained, interactive HTML report of their results.


Who is the developer of floraR?
Development is led by JBRJ, with financial support from CNPq and FINEP. Main developer:

Domingos Cardoso (@DBOSlab)

View the code and contribute on GitHub: https://github.com/DBOSlab/floraR


Why the name floraR?
The name pairs “Flora” — for Flora e Funga do Brasil, the checklist it interfaces with — with the R programming language, reflecting the package’s goal of making the national checklist directly and reproducibly accessible from R.


Where can I report bugs or request features?
Submit issues on GitHub: floraR Issues.


Where can I ask questions and discuss floraR?
Join our community via GitHub Discussions to ask questions, suggest ideas, or help others.


How does floraR relate to Flora e Funga do Brasil?
The floraR package is a programmatic interface to the Flora e Funga do Brasil IPT data portal: it downloads, parses, and queries the same checklist data published on the platform, and also helps taxonomic experts prepare new names and records for contribution back to it.


Can I contribute new names or records to Flora e Funga do Brasil?
Yes. floraR includes tools specifically to help taxonomic experts expand FFB: flora_species_gap() lists species recorded in Brazil but missing from FFB, flora_distribution_gap() lists candidate new state records, and flora_get_descriptions() and flora_build_matrix() pull controlled-field and free-text descriptions from existing FFB taxon pages and turn them into a comparable trait matrix. To submit new names or corrections to the platform itself, see the contribution guidelines at floradobrasil.jbrj.gov.br/consulta or contact the FFB coordination team at floraefungadobrasil@jbrj.gov.br.

title: Download the FFB checklist
text: Here we present a practical guide to the flora_download() function of the floraR package. This function downloads taxonomic and distributional records from the Flora e Funga do Brasil (FFB) platform in Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A) format, directly from the FFB IPT data portal.

title: Download the FFB checklist
text:
Function Overview
flora_download() retrieves one or more versions of the FFB dataset and saves each one to its own subdirectory on disk. It checks whether a requested version is already present locally and avoids re-downloading it unnecessarily, so it is safe to call repeatedly across a project.

title: Download the FFB checklist
text:
Arguments







Argument
Description




version
Character. "latest" (default) downloads the most recent release; "all" downloads every available version (large!); a version string or vector of version strings (e.g. "393.418") downloads specific releases. Use flora_version() to inspect valid version numbers first.


verbose
Logical. If TRUE (default), prints informative messages during download.


dir
Character. Local directory to save the downloaded files. Defaults to "flora_download". Each version is extracted into its own subdirectory.

title: Download the FFB checklist
text:
Download the latest dataset
library(floraR)

flora_download(dir = "flora_download")

title: Download the FFB checklist
text:
Download a specific version
Use flora_version() first to find a valid version string:
versions_df <- flora_version()

flora_download(version = versions_df$Version[1], dir = "flora_download")

title: Download the FFB checklist
text:
Download multiple versions
flora_download(version = c("393.418", "392.417"), dir = "flora_download")

title: Download the FFB checklist
text:
Download every available version
# Large download! Only needed for archival or cross-version comparisons.
flora_download(version = "all", dir = "flora_download")

title: Download the FFB checklist
text:
Additional Tips

You rarely need to call flora_download() directly: flora_records(), flora_search(), flora_match(), flora_get_children_taxa(), flora_species_gap(), and flora_distribution_gap() all download and cache the dataset automatically the first time you call them.
If no internet connection is available, flora_download() automatically falls back to a previously downloaded local copy, if one exists in dir.
Keep the downloaded folder (the default rm_flora_database = FALSE behavior in downstream functions) so that repeated analyses reuse the cache instead of re-downloading the archive every time.

title: Check available FFB dataset versions
text:
Here we present a practical guide to the flora_version() function of the floraR package. This function retrieves metadata about the dataset versions of the Flora e Funga do Brasil (FFB) checklist currently published on the FFB IPT data portal, hosted by the Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden.
Because FFB is a living checklist, continuously updated as taxonomists review and add names, every dataset release is versioned. Checking which versions exist — and which one is current — is normally the first step before downloading, parsing, or filtering FFB data, since it lets you pin your analysis to a specific, citable release.

title: Check available FFB dataset versions
text:
Function Overview
flora_version() takes no arguments: it simply queries the FFB IPT metadata and returns a data frame summarizing every published version.

title: Check available FFB dataset versions
text:
Output columns







Column
Description




Version
Version number of the dataset release.


Published_on
Timestamp of the dataset release.


Records
Number of records included in the release.


URL
Direct link to the dataset version on the IPT portal.


Latest
Logical. TRUE for the row corresponding to the most recently published version.

title: Check available FFB dataset versions
text:
List all available versions
library(floraR)

versions_df <- flora_version()
head(versions_df)

title: Check available FFB dataset versions
text:
Identify the latest version
latest <- versions_df[versions_df$Latest == TRUE, ]
latest$Version

flora_download() and flora_parse(), and every function built on top of them (flora_records(), flora_search(), flora_match(), flora_get_children_taxa(), flora_species_gap(), flora_distribution_gap()), default to version = "latest". You only need flora_version() directly when you want to pin an analysis to a specific, older release for reproducibility.
Pass a specific version string from the Version column (e.g. flora_download(version = versions_df$Version[1])) to work with that exact release instead of the current one.
The Records column is a quick way to sanity-check that a download completed correctly: the number of parsed rows should be in the same order of magnitude.

title: Explore the taxonomic hierarchy
text: Here we present a practical guide to the flora_get_children_taxa() function of the floraR package. It retrieves all child taxa — species, subspecies, varieties, and so on — below a given taxonomic name and rank, which is useful for getting every species in a genus, every genus in a family, and similar hierarchy traversals.

title: Explore the taxonomic hierarchy
text:
Function Overview
flora_get_children_taxa() first locates the parent taxon in the Flora e Funga do Brasil (FFB) checklist, then returns every taxon whose lineage includes that parent’s taxon ID.

title: Explore the taxonomic hierarchy
text:
Arguments







Argument
Description




taxon_name
Character. Scientific name to search for (e.g. "Luetzelburgia", "Fabaceae", "Magnoliopsida").


rank
Character. Taxonomic rank of taxon_name: "class", "order", "family", "genus", or "species". Default "genus".


child_rank
Character or NULL. Rank(s) to return as children. NULL (default) returns all descendant ranks; a single rank (e.g. "species") restricts the result to that rank only.


include_synonyms
Logical. If TRUE, includes synonym names in addition to accepted ones. Default FALSE.


version
FFB dataset version to use. Defaults to "latest".


rm_flora_database
If TRUE, deletes the cached database after the search. Default FALSE is recommended for repeated use.


verbose
Logical. If TRUE (default), prints progress messages.

title: Explore the taxonomic hierarchy
section: Get all species in a genus
text:
Get all species in a genus
library(floraR)

species <- flora_get_children_taxa(taxon_name = "Luetzelburgia",
                                   rank = "genus",
                                   child_rank = "species")

title: Explore the taxonomic hierarchy
section: Get every descendant of a genus
text:
Get every descendant of a genus
Species, subspecies, and varieties together:
all_descendants <- flora_get_children_taxa(taxon_name = "Luetzelburgia",
                                           rank = "genus",
                                           child_rank = NULL)

title: Explore the taxonomic hierarchy
section: Get all genera in a family, including synonyms
text:
Get all genera in a family, including synonyms
genera <- flora_get_children_taxa(taxon_name = "Fabaceae",
                                  rank = "family",
                                  child_rank = "genus",
                                  include_synonyms = TRUE)

title: Explore the taxonomic hierarchy
text:
Additional Tips

Set child_rank = NULL when you want a complete picture of a group’s diversity, including infraspecific taxa; set it to a single rank (e.g. "species") when you specifically need a species-level checklist for downstream work.
rank must correctly describe taxon_name (e.g. don’t pass a genus name with rank = "family") — the function looks up the parent by matching both together.
Combine with flora_records() when you need geographic or trait filters in addition to hierarchy traversal (e.g. all species in a genus that are also endemic to a given state).

title: Filter and retrieve checklist records
text: Here we present a practical guide to the flora_records() function of the floraR package. Unlike flora_search() and flora_match(), which resolve a list of names you already have against the checklist, flora_records() browses and filters the Flora e Funga do Brasil (FFB) checklist directly — no input name list required.

title: Filter and retrieve checklist records
text:
Function Overview
flora_records() downloads and parses the FFB dataset automatically (like flora_search(), reusing the local cache on repeated calls), then applies whichever combination of taxonomic, geographic, and trait-based filters you request. All filters are combined with a logical AND, and the result always has one row per matching taxon.

title: Filter and retrieve checklist records
text:
Arguments







Argument
Description




taxon
Character vector. One or more family, genus, or species names to filter by (e.g. c("Fabaceae", "Luetzelburgia", "Inga edulis")).


taxonRank
Character vector. Taxonomic rank(s) to keep (e.g. "ESPECIE", "VARIEDADE", "SUBESPECIE").


taxonomicStatus
Character vector. FFB taxonomic status: "NOME_ACEITO" (accepted), "SINONIMO" (synonym), or "NOME_DUVIDOSO" (doubtful).


state
Character vector. Brazilian state(s), full name or acronym, diacritics-insensitive (e.g. "Bahia" or "BA").


phytogeographicDomain
Character vector. Phytogeographic domain(s) (e.g. "Caatinga", "Mata Atlantica").


endemism
Logical. TRUE keeps only Brazilian endemics; FALSE keeps only non-endemics.


lifeForm, habitat, vegetationType
Character vectors. Life form (e.g. "Arbusto"), habitat (e.g. "Terricola") and vegetation type (e.g. "Cerrado (lato sensu)").


version
Character. FFB dataset version to use. Defaults to "latest".


rm_flora_database
Logical. If TRUE, deletes the downloaded database after the search. Default FALSE keeps it cached for faster repeated queries.


verbose
Logical. If TRUE (default), prints progress messages.


save
Logical. If TRUE, writes the filtered records to a CSV file.


dir, filename
Where and under what name to save the CSV when save = TRUE.

title: Filter and retrieve checklist records
text:
Browse a whole family
library(floraR)

fabaceae <- flora_records(taxon = "Fabaceae",
                          taxonomicStatus = "NOME_ACEITO")

title: Filter and retrieve checklist records
text:
Filter by state and endemism
bahia_endemics <- flora_records(state = "Bahia",
                                endemism = TRUE,
                                taxonomicStatus = "NOME_ACEITO")

title: Filter and retrieve checklist records
section: Filter by phytogeographic domain and life form
text:
Filter by phytogeographic domain and life form
caatinga_shrubs <- flora_records(phytogeographicDomain = "Caatinga",
                                 lifeForm = "Arbusto")

title: Filter and retrieve checklist records
section: Save the result to a CSV file
text:
Save the result to a CSV file
flora_records(taxon = "Luetzelburgia",
             save = TRUE,
             dir = "flora_records",
             filename = "luetzelburgia_records")

title: Filter and retrieve checklist records
text:
Additional Tips

taxon is matched against the family, genus and taxonName columns automatically — a family name ending in "aceae", a single-word genus, or a multi-word species name are all detected and matched appropriately.
Combine multiple filters freely: they are always ANDed together, so flora_records(taxon = "Fabaceae", state = "Bahia", endemism = TRUE) returns Fabaceae species endemic to Bahia.
If you already have your own species list to resolve rather than browse the checklist by criteria, use flora_search() or flora_match() instead.

title: floraR
text:
Flora e Funga do Brasil
Brazil harbors the richest plant, algal, and fungal diversity in the world (BFG 2022). Assembling a complete, continuously updated checklist of this diversity has been a decades-long collaborative effort involving hundreds of taxonomists across the country.
The project began in 2008 as the Lista de Espécies da Flora do Brasil, a first attempt to compile a national species checklist validated by specialists. It evolved into Flora do Brasil 2020, launched to meet Brazil’s commitments under the Global Strategy for Plant Conservation of the Convention on Biological Diversity, and — following the incorporation of fungi — into its current form, Flora e Funga do Brasil.
For each accepted name, the checklist records nomenclatural status (accepted, synonym, or doubtful), taxonomic classification, geographic distribution across Brazilian states and phytogeographic domains, endemism status, life form, habitat, and vegetation type. This structured, validated backbone underpins taxonomic research, conservation assessments, and biodiversity informatics across the country, and is also the nomenclatural reference used to validate specimen images published on the Reflora Virtual Herbarium.
Data are published as versioned Darwin Core Archives through the FFB IPT Data Portal, hosted by the Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden (JBRJ). floraR reads directly from this portal, so every result reflects the checklist as curated by the taxonomist community at the time of the query.
If you are a taxonomist and wish to contribute new names, updates, or corrections to Flora e Funga do Brasil, see the contribution guidelines on the platform itself, or contact the FFB coordination team at floraefungadobrasil@jbrj.gov.br.

title: Explorar a hierarquia taxonômica
text: Aqui apresentamos um guia prático para a função flora_get_children_taxa() do pacote floraR. Ela recupera todos os táxons filhos — espécies, subespécies, variedades e assim por diante — abaixo de um nome e nível taxonômico especificados, o que é útil para obter todas as espécies de um gênero, todos os gêneros de uma família, e outras travessias de hierarquia semelhantes.

title: Explorar a hierarquia taxonômica
text:
Visão Geral da Função
A flora_get_children_taxa() primeiro localiza o táxon pai na lista de espécies da Flora e Funga do Brasil (FFB), e então retorna todo táxon cuja linhagem inclua o ID de táxon desse pai.

title: Explorar a hierarquia taxonômica
text:
Argumentos







Argumento
Descrição




taxon_name
Caractere. Nome científico a buscar (ex.: "Luetzelburgia", "Fabaceae", "Magnoliopsida").


rank
Caractere. Nível taxonômico de taxon_name: "class", "order", "family", "genus", ou "species". Padrão "genus".


child_rank
Caractere ou NULL. Nível(is) a retornar como filhos. NULL (padrão) retorna todos os níveis descendentes; um único nível (ex.: "species") restringe o resultado apenas a esse nível.


include_synonyms
Lógico. Se TRUE, inclui nomes sinônimos além dos aceitos. Padrão FALSE.


version
Versão do conjunto de dados da FFB a usar. Padrão "latest".


rm_flora_database
Se TRUE, exclui o banco de dados em cache após a busca. O padrão FALSE é recomendado para uso repetido.


verbose
Lógico. Se TRUE (padrão), imprime mensagens de progresso.

title: floraR
text:
Flora e Funga do Brasil
O Brasil abriga a maior diversidade de plantas, algas e fungos do mundo (BFG 2022). Reunir uma lista de espécies completa e continuamente atualizada dessa diversidade tem sido um esforço colaborativo de décadas, envolvendo centenas de taxonomistas em todo o país.
O projeto começou em 2008 como a Lista de Espécies da Flora do Brasil, uma primeira tentativa de compilar uma lista nacional de espécies validada por especialistas. Evoluiu para o Flora do Brasil 2020, lançado para atender aos compromissos do Brasil com a Estratégia Global para a Conservação das Plantas da Convenção sobre Diversidade Biológica, e — após a incorporação dos fungos — para sua forma atual, Flora e Funga do Brasil.
Para cada nome aceito, a lista de espécies registra o status nomenclatural (aceito, sinônimo ou duvidoso), a classificação taxonômica, a distribuição geográfica entre estados brasileiros e domínios fitogeográficos, o status de endemismo, a forma de vida, o hábitat e o tipo de vegetação. Essa base taxonômica estruturada e validada sustenta a pesquisa taxonômica, as avaliações de conservação e a informática da biodiversidade em todo o país, sendo também a referência nomenclatural usada para validar as imagens de espécimes publicadas no Herbário Virtual Reflora.
Os dados são publicados como Arquivos Darwin Core versionados através do Portal de Dados IPT da FFB, hospedado pelo Jardim Botânico do Rio de Janeiro (JBRJ). O floraR lê diretamente desse portal, de modo que cada resultado reflete a lista de espécies tal como curada pela comunidade de taxonomistas no momento da consulta.
Se você é taxonomista e deseja contribuir com novos nomes, atualizações ou correções para a Flora e Funga do Brasil, consulte as diretrizes de contribuição na própria plataforma, ou entre em contato com a equipe de coordenação da FFB pelo e-mail floraefungadobrasil@jbrj.gov.br.

title: Novidades
text:
Lançamento Inicial
Primeira versão oficial do pacote R floraR, desenvolvido para oferecer ferramentas completas de acesso, análise e curadoria de dados da plataforma Flora e Funga do Brasil (FFB), hospedada pelo Jardim Botânico do Rio de Janeiro.

Funcionalidades

flora_version(): Recupera metadados e verifica as versões disponíveis do conjunto de dados no portal IPT da FFB.
flora_download(): Baixa dados taxonômicos e de distribuição em formato Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A) para versões específicas ou todas as disponíveis.
flora_parse(): Analisa e organiza conjuntos de dados da FFB baixados localmente em uma lista de tabelas pronta para uso.
flora_records(): Navega e filtra a lista de espécies da FFB diretamente por critérios taxonômicos, geográficos e de atributos, sem exigir uma lista de nomes de entrada.
flora_search(): Resolve sua própria lista de nomes de espécies em relação à lista de espécies da FFB, com correspondência exata primeiro e correspondência aproximada (distância de Levenshtein) como alternativa para erros de digitação, incluindo resolução de sinônimos.
flora_match(): Compara duas listas independentes de nomes de espécies, alinhando nomes que resolvem para o mesmo táxon aceito.
flora_get_children_taxa(): Recupera todos os táxons filhos (espécies, subespécies, variedades etc.) abaixo de um nome e nível taxonômico especificados.
flora_get_descriptions(): Extrai descrições de campos controlados e texto livre de páginas de táxons da FFB, para auxiliar especialistas na curadoria de novos registros.
flora_build_matrix(): Transforma as descrições de táxons extraídas em uma matriz de caracteres por táxon.
A maioria das funções baixa e analisa o conjunto de dados da FFB automaticamente e o armazena em cache local, de modo que consultas repetidas e análises offline funcionam sem a necessidade de novo download.
Integração completa com fluxos de trabalho do tidyverse para análises posteriores.
Conjunto abrangente de testes com testthat, integração contínua via GitHub Actions.
